title: Globo della Terra di tre piedi, e mezzo di diametro - printed gores and polar calottes
creator: Vincenzo Maria Coronelli
publication_context: Venice, Accademia Cosmografica degli Argonauti; 24 gores and 2 polar calottes for a terrestrial globe of 42 inches (107 cm) diameter
edition_state: David Rumsey copy of the State Library of New South Wales set, publication 10070; south polar calotte list no. 10070.026, north polar calotte 10070.025
dimensions: Calotte 36 x 36 cm; assembled globe 107 cm diameter; scale 1:11,458,33
repository: State Library of New South Wales (the printed gores); David Rumsey Historical Map Collection (the images)
scan_source: David Rumsey IIIF image service, 13744 x 13850; south polar calotte examined at full resolution 2026-08-27. Images provided by the State Library of New South Wales, where the original printed gores reside.
role_in_essay: Coronelli's world in the round, and the one southern surface he could not leave blank without leaving a hole.
notes: Located and examined 2026-08-27, replacing the Rumsey blog record that stood here as a placeholder. The south polar calotte carries no land at all: meridians radiating from the pole and concentric parallels, and no coastline anywhere on the cap. The title is engraved around the pole as 'POLO ANTARTICO O SIA MERIDIONALE'. The space is filled instead by a large allegorical cartouche whose text is a narrative of Magellan - 237 men from Charles V, five ships out of Seville on 10 August 1519, the strait found on 31 March, the Vittoria home in 1522 after 14,460 leagues - and, around the rim and in a left-hand panel headed 'Del Sito, Distanza, Divisione, e Differenti Habitatori della Terra', the five climatic zones and their inhabitants. Those are the only two prose blocks on the sheet. This is the constraint argument's best evidence: on a globe the southern cap must be engraved with something, and what Coronelli engraved there was history and cosmographical apparatus rather than conjectured coast, which is the same judgement the Atlante Veneto essay makes in words at printed p. 75. rights_status records the 1688 work, not the scan: reproduction_use stays undetermined because the images are supplied by the State Library of New South Wales and their terms have not been read. review_status stays source_checked; the record has been read but not reviewed by a person.

title: Terre Artiche
creator: Vincenzo Maria Coronelli
publication_context: Atlante Veneto, Tomo I, Venice; Rumsey publication 12186, plate 12186.101
edition_state: David Rumsey copy, list no. 12186.101; plate state not further established
scan_source: David Rumsey IIIF image service, 12365 x 7744; plate examined at full resolution 2026-08-25
role_in_essay: The plate Act III actually has: a north polar sheet crowded with named voyages, set against a southern polar section that received no plate at all.
notes: Examined 2026-08-25 at full IIIF resolution: Arctic to the neatline, north polar azimuthal projection on a double-page spread, with the gutter falling through the pole. Dedication cartouche to Conte Ercole Pepoli, Senator of Bologna and Venetian patrician. The legend inside the central mountain ring records Hugh Willoughby ('Vgone Willogheo') at 76 degrees, a Spitsbergen overwintering party of seven that sailed 30 August 1633 and returned without profit 26 May 1634, and Friedrich Martens of Hamburg, who left the Elbe 15 April 1671 and returned 21 August the same year having reached 81 degrees. Replaces the former ant-obj-coronelli-terre-polari, whose persistent_id resolved to Rumsey 1012.002, a 1929 Touring Club Italiano plate; no Coronelli map plate of that title exists in the Rumsey catalogue. Reproduction stays undetermined: the object is verified, but clearing a plate for DeepZoom is a publication decision and the pilot's public tier is empty until a person reviews the record. Tied to the text 2026-08-25: Friedrich Martens's 1671 Spitsbergen voyage appears both in this plate's central legend and in the accompanying essay at printed p. 73 and in its closing source list at p. 76, which is the plate and the text resting on one named source.

title: Map of the Antarctic continent, in the Atlas of the Narrative of the United States Exploring Expedition
creator: Charles Wilkes; United States Exploring Expedition
publication_context: Atlas of the Narrative of the United States Exploring Expedition during the years 1838, 1839, 1840, 1841, 1842. Philadelphia: C. Sherman, 1844
edition_state: Atlas plate No. 70; 5 profile views on the same sheet
repository: Library of Congress, Geography and Map Division
scan_source: Library of Congress digitised copy 3, shelf g9230m.gct00224 (persistent_id above); the LoC site itself returns a bot-detection challenge from this environment, so the plate was examined at full IIIF resolution via the American Geographical Society Library’s digitised copy of the same plate (University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee Libraries, Digital ID am004598, https://collections.lib.uwm.edu/digital/collection/agdm/id/12243/) instead.
role_in_essay: Charted coast, some of which was later sailed through: the bridge from Act V into Act VI.
notes: Plate examined 2026-08-27: “Chart of the Antarctic Continent Shewing the Icy Barrier Attached to it, Discovered by the U.S. Ex.Ex. Charles Wilkes Esq. Commander, 1840,” plate/sheet No. 70. “Termination Land” is named on it, drawn with a dotted (unsurveyed) coastline convention rather than the solid line used for surveyed coast, in the chart’s western sector near Knox’s and Budd’s High Land and Repulse Bay. Approximate position read off the plate’s own graticule: about 94.5-96.7°E, 67.9-70.1°S (centre roughly 95.6°E, 69.0°S). Read from the plate's own graticule (pixel position against the top-edge longitude ticks and the left/right-edge latitude ticks, both legible and internally consistent at two check points each), not a formal georeference with control points – treat as approximate, not survey-grade. This is the position ant-gap-wilkes-sheets asked for and ant-ghost-wilkes-segment cites; it is not the 65-67°S/160-165°E figure that had been circulating for ‘Termination Land’ before this plate was actually opened – that figure, if it belongs to anything on this chart, is closer to the more easterly cluster of named peaks (Ringgold’s Knoll and neighbours), not Termination Land, which was not independently re-checked here.

creator: HM Admiralty; Robert Christopher Carrington; Malby and Son
publication_context: Admiralty chart; polar projection to latitude 30 degrees south
dimensions: Sheet 68 x 68 cm; print, partially coloured
role_in_essay: The 1910 chart's predecessor, and the evidence that a cumulative synthesis is itself revised.
notes: Catalogue record read during the ANT-8 audit. The decisive comparison: this title's voyage list ends at Ross 1841-2-3 and adds Towson's iceberg papers of 1855-59, while the 1910 sheet adds Scott 1901-4 and Shackleton 1908-9. Two catalogue titles, one revision, and Act VII's layered archive stops being a metaphor. Crown copyright applies.

title: Atlas plates from Voyage au Pole Sud et dans l'Oceanie (exact plates to be identified)
creator: Jules Sebastien Cesar Dumont d'Urville
publication_context: Paris: Gide; atlas accompanying the narrative
edition_state: Atlas pittoresque, T. 2 (Paris, 1846); plates 168-172 confirmed present
scan_source: Heidelberg University Library digitisation, DOI 10.11588/diglit.20229 (Atlas pittoresque T. 2)
role_in_essay: A third national chart of the same 1840 coast, alongside Wilkes and Ross.
notes: Gallica blocks this environment (bot-detection challenge on both a plain fetch and a browser tab), but Heidelberg University Library holds its own free digitisation of the atlas and does not: confirmed 2026-08-27 via https://digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/diglit/dumont1841ga, which lists four digitised items – the two narrative text volumes and Atlas pittoresque T. 1 and T. 2. Plates 168-172 (the plate range the Terre Adelie landing sequence is reported at) all exist in T. 2 and were opened one by one via the viewer''s plate-jump control; each carries a printed "PL. <n>" watermark confirming its number, and 168 shows a ship/landing scene consistent with a Terre Adelie plate. Individual plate captions were not transcribed (the viewer does not expose OCR text and this was not read caption-by-caption), so this is partially_verified rather than verified. No "Atlas Hydrographique" volume with the technical charts (the plate the essay would need for actual coastline positions rather than illustrated scenes) is among Heidelberg''s four digitised items; that volume remains unlocated.
